scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Sometimes a loop should stop early, or skip a round. Today we meet three tools that give you more control.

scenes.onScreen: "Control inside a loop": three numbered lines (1. break leaves the loop now; 2. continue skips to the next round; 3. else runs only if the loop was never broken) and an analogy card: a bus journey: break gets off the bus now, continue skips this stop, and else means you reached the end
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Inside a loop, three tools give you more control. Break leaves the loop at once. Continue skips the rest of this round, and goes to the next. And else, after the loop, runs only when the loop finished without a break. Think of a bus journey. Break means get off the bus right now. Continue means skip this stop. Else means you reached the last stop.

scenes.onScreen: stop_at.py: a loop that stops when n is 4
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right; faint indent guide lines
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A loop over one to nine. [HL 2] An if inside the loop. When n is four, [HL 3] we print a message, [HL 4] and break. Break ends the whole loop at once. [HL 5] For other values, this line prints. It is at the same level as the if, so it runs when the if does not.

scenes.onScreen: After the break, the name n stays tied to 4
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is what is left after the break. The name n is tied to the int four, the value it had when the loop was left. The loop never reached five. Compare that with a loop that finishes normally, where the name ends on the last value in the series. This is a handy way to see where a loop stopped.

scenes.onScreen: odds.py: skip even numbers; else runs because there was no break
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A loop over one to five. [HL 2] If n is even, remainder zero when divided by two, [HL 3] we continue. That skips the rest of this round. [HL 4] Odd numbers reach this line and print. [HL 5] Now the loop else. [HL 6] It runs only when the loop was not broken. Here there was no break, so it prints.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: break leaves the loop immediately. Two: continue skips the rest of the current round. Three: A loop else runs only when the loop ended without a break. Four: In a while loop, update the counter before you continue. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: continue skips the update
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We want to skip the number two. But when n is two, continue jumps back to the top, and skips the line that adds one. So n stays two forever, and the program hangs after printing zero and one. With a while loop, add one before you continue. Then the loop moves on.

bug.fixed:
n = 0
while n < 5:
    if n == 2:
        n = n + 1
        continue
    print(n)
    n = n + 1
bug.why: continue jumps straight back to the condition, so a counter update placed after it is skipped and the loop never ends.

shorts.title: Break
shorts.script: Break leaves a loop immediately. Say you are searching for a number. The moment you find it, you do not need to keep looking. So you write break, and Python jumps out of the loop and carries on with the next line. Think of a bus journey. Break means, I am getting off right now. It makes searches faster and your code simpler. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Stop a loop early.

shorts.title: Continue
shorts.hook: "Continue skips the rest of the current round, and goes straight to the next one."
shorts.script: Continue skips the rest of the current round, and goes straight to the next one. Say you only want to print odd numbers. When a number is even, you write continue. Python skips the print for that round, and moves on. It is like skipping a stop on a bus route. The bus keeps going, and only this stop is missed. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Skip one round.

shorts.title: Loop else
shorts.script: Here is a very Python feature. A loop can have an else. It runs only when the loop finished without hitting a break. So if you search for something, and the loop ends normally, the else tells you that nothing was found. It is like reaching the last stop of the bus route. It is rare in other languages, but very handy here. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Else runs without a break.

shorts.title: Continue and the counter
shorts.script: A tricky bug. In a while loop, you write continue before the line that adds one to the counter. When the condition is met, continue jumps back to the top, and the counter never changes. The loop hangs on that value forever. The fix is to update the counter before you continue. Always check where your update line sits. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Update first.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the loop get off the bus early?"
shorts.script: Why did the loop get off the bus early? It heard someone say break. Your challenge. Loop from one to ten, and print each number. But stop the loop as soon as you reach seven, using break. You should see only the numbers one to six. Then change break to continue, and see what changes. Tell us what you notice. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 18.
